source.book: The Art and Science of Technical Analysis
source.author: Adam Grimes

conventions: stop and limit entries mechanized as bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode; price-level conditions rejected (shift test)

candidates.name: MinStopDistanceAverageBarRange
candidates.quote: A rough guideline is given by the average range of a single bar on the time frame you are trading. If you try to place your initial stops closer than one average bar's range, you are probably working within the noise level...
candidates.description: The initial protective stop, wherever the pattern otherwise places it, should never sit closer to the entry than the average range of a single bar on the trading time frame (approximated by ATR). This is a floor on stop distance, not a stop-placement method by itself: if the pattern-based stop distance is smaller than the average bar range, widen it to at least the average range.

complexity.reason: a window loop into ATR over N bars, then a max() against whatever other stop-distance rule supplies the pattern-based distance

notes: Grimes gives no explicit lookback for 'average range of a single bar'; defaulted atrLength to 14 (a common ATR default) since he does not name one here.

This is a floor/guardrail on other stop rules, not a standalone stop-placement rule; the authoring pass may prefer to fold it into existing ATR-stop rules as a minimum-distance clamp rather than a new standalone rule.

chapter_summary: Chapter 9 is almost entirely position sizing (Kelly criterion, fixed-fractional vs. fixed-dollar risk, extensive Monte Carlo comparisons) and portfolio-level risk (correlation, liquidity, tail/event, regulatory, execution, disaster risk), none of which reduces to a bar-level OHLCV test and all of which is recorded under rejected with reason 'position sizing' or the relevant no-bar-data reason. The one genuine bar-level statement is the guideline that an initial stop should never be placed closer than the market's average single-bar range -- a floor/clamp on stop distance, mechanized here as an ATR-based minimum applied to whatever pattern-based stop distance is otherwise chosen.
